newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FEATURE - Ivory Coast laments lost forest.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ivory Coast laments lost forest.

text.p: "Trees, Environment and Life" -- the themes of Ivory Coast's National Tree Day -- were simple.
But saving Ivory Coast's rainforest has proved a hard target as slash-and-burn farming and illegal logging continue to destroy protected and other forest areas.
A symbolic sapling planted at last year's event by President Henri Konan Bedie has gained a few inches but a wider replanting plan has borne little fruit.

This year, the duty fell to Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan who planted his tree on July 31 against a sombre background of just 1,000 hectares (2,471 acres) replanted in 1996 under the slogan "One Ivorian, One Tree."
"All the results remain below the targets hoped for," said Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan.
Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, with a population of more than 14 million, aims to replant 70 percent of its forests.
Tree cover has dwindled with rising cocoa output and logging to around 3.9 million hectares (9.6 million acres) from 12 million hectares (29.7 million acres) before independence from France in 1960.
FORESTRY AGENTS TO BURN OUT ILLEGAL FARMERS

Ivory Coast has raised the temperature in its efforts to save forests, evicting some cocoa and coffee farmers from protected forests and telling those remaining they face being burnt out from August. But harvesting is likely to continue in protected areas for several years during a transition period.

"We told farmers they must leave or we will burn them out, said a forestry agency official with the state Societe de Developpement des Forets (SODEFOR) near a shanty camp for ousted farmers. "Our patrols show a lot have left but there are no figures."
Migrant cocoa farmers fleeing southern coastal forests said SODEFOR agents gave them two months notice to quit farms in May.
"They said we could go back and harvest what was on trees but not plant any more stock," said 24-year-old Sirike, who plans to move from the area.

The government has said 30 percent of protected forests was "illegally occupied" by up to 450,000 farmers and their relatives, growing up to 100,000 tonnes of cocoa -- or roughly a tenth of the 1996/97 crop of nearly 1.1 million tonnes.
Protected forest farms often yield small crops.
Husbandry is usually poor -- around 0.3 tonnes a hectare compared to 0.5 upwards in normal farms -- as uncertain land ownership discourages farmers from putting in much effort.
"On older plantations it is difficult to make people leave," said a south coast manager for SODEFOR, the Ministry of Agriculture agency tasked with carrying out the policy.
Ivory Coast produces about 40 percent of the world's cocoa but wants to cut output to shore up long-term world prices.
"You can still see in the forest clearings operations going on," said one donor official visiting thinning forest areas.
"It's a socio-economic phenomenon that seems uncontrollable."
SODEFOR has set up dozens of seedling plantations in forest areas but the government says more private sector involvement is needed for replanting to succeed.
ANGRY DONORS CUT FORESTRY FUNDING
Donors have grown weary of broken promises on forestry policy and from July witheld funding for donor-dependent SODEFOR, which has 400 field staff and 828 administrators.

Ivory Coast produced two million cubic metres of timber in 1996 against the four million cubic metres a year target set under a 1988-96 plan. Only German donor funds will remain after African Development Bank forestry support ends in late 1997.

Donors say illegal logging has continued and want to see tax benefits to encourage protection of rare trees. Exports of tropical timber to many western markets, including the EU, have already been banned.
"This is a very serious problem for Ivory Coast," said one donor, pointing to the effect on gross domestic product, export revenue and the country's overall trade balance.

Illegal, tax-evading saw mills have since sprung up in the southwestern port of San Pedro. The port borders on the Tai National Park, a UNESCO-designated World Heritage site where rare animals and organisms, including a strain of the deadly Ebola virus have been found.

Community workers say Tai planters have been injured by fire during the destruction of 20 villages and farms over the past six months, even before the government announced its eviction policy in March.
CONSERVATION THROUGH OWNERSHIP?
Ivorian land law is generally unclear.
Founding president Felix Houphouet-Boigny gave planters title to land they planted but the government says those who settled in forests protected from 1973 have no title.
Ivory Coast took steps to clarify land title in August with new laws aimed at defining ownership of all rural areas outside classified forests and existing public and urban spaces.

In one 12,437 hectare forest cocoa production had taken over 2,500 hectares, with yields of 0.3 tonnes a hectare, forestry agents said. Coffee farms covered 206 hectares, producing one tonne a hectare but only 50 hectares of forest had been replanted.
Land holders now have three years to submit a case for registered title, with unattributed land passing to the state.

Local agricultural analysts say that could help avoid a "Tragedy of the Commons" -- a phenomenon seen in open access resources where a lack of ownership removes incentives for all to make conservation efforts.
Others are less optimistic, citing local officials with illegal plantations who evict farmers getting in their way.
"There could be no forest left at all in 10 years," one said.
